lesson.menu_title: Have You Ever — The Convention Conversation
lesson.menu_desc: Ever, never, already and yet, in the twenty minutes between two sessions -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- Have You Ever
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosa M. Mitiko Shida | Lesson 4 -- Have You Ever
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect with ever, never, already and yet

listenings.text: Good morning and welcome to the regional commercial convention. A few practical points before the first session. Coffee is on the second floor, not on this one, and the coffee breaks are twenty minutes, which is shorter than usual because the programme is full. If you have never been to one of our regional events before, there are about ninety of us here, from four countries, and the working language is English for everything except the corridor. Your name badge has a coloured line at the bottom. Blue means commercial, green means operations, orange means you are a guest. Use it. It is the fastest icebreaker in the building.

I have been coming to these events for eleven years and I have learned exactly one thing that matters, so I will give it to you now. Do not try to meet everybody. In twenty minutes you can have one real conversation or six terrible ones, and the six will give you nothing. Find one person you have never spoken to, ask them something you actually want to know, and stay there. If they are interesting, say so, and ask for their email before you walk away. That is it. I have never once regretted a conversation I stayed in, and I have forgotten every single person I met for ninety seconds.

reading.rtitle: The Twenty Minutes That Decide the Convention
paras: Everybody who has ever attended an industry convention knows the feeling. The session ends, four hundred people stand up at the same time, and there are twenty minutes before the next one. Somewhere in that room is the person who will call you in March about a contract. You have never met them and you have no way of knowing who they are.

The instinct is to move fast and collect. Shake hands, hand over a card, say the name of your company, move on. It feels productive and it almost never works. Nobody has ever built a working relationship out of ninety seconds and a business card, and everybody who has tried has the same drawer full of cards from people they cannot place.

The people who get the most out of these events do something that looks lazy. They talk to two people, for ten minutes each, and they ask questions they genuinely want answered. They have already decided that six weak conversations are worth less than one real one. It is not a social skill. It is arithmetic.

And there is one more thing they all do, which costs nothing. Before they walk away, they say what happens next. Send me that report. I will introduce you to the person who handles Chile. Are you coming to the dinner? A conversation that ends without a next step has not really happened, however good it was.
reading.source: Column -- South America Commercial Aviation Review

gist.prompt: What is this column mainly about?
choices: Why industry conventions are a waste of time
Why two long conversations beat six short ones, and how to close them
How to design the programme of a convention

items: The column says you should meet as many people as possible in the break.
Nobody has ever built a working relationship out of ninety seconds and a business card.
The people who get the most out of conventions talk to fewer people, for longer.
They talk to two people, for ten minutes each, and they ask questions they genuinely want answered.
The column calls this a social skill.
It is not a social skill. It is arithmetic.
Saying what happens next is optional, according to the column.
A conversation that ends without a next step has not really happened, however good it was.

items.situation: You are standing alone with a coffee. Somebody with an orange badge is standing alone next to you.
tips: The badge is the icebreaker -- ask about it
Have you been to one of these before?

items.situation: Somebody asks whether you have ever worked on a route launch.
tips: Answer with ever or never, then add one detail
If never, say what you have done instead

items.situation: A colleague from Santiago asks whether you have met the new regional director.
tips: Already if yes, not yet if no
Add where or when you expect to

items.situation: The conversation is going well and the break is nearly over.
tips: Close with a next step, not with goodbye
Could I send you that? / Are you coming to the dinner?

items.situation: Somebody asks a question about operations and you do not know the answer.
tips: Say so, then offer the person who does
I have never handled that side -- let me introduce you to somebody who has

items.situation: You run into a client you have not seen since the pandemic.
tips: Say how long it has been
I have not seen you since 2019 -- how has the business been?

extra_audio.text: Andres introduces himself and says he has seen her name on the regional list but has never met her. Rosa says which office she works in and asks whether he has been to this convention before. Andres answers that he has attended it three times and explains what he has learned about the coffee breaks. Rosa asks whether he has already met the new regional director, and Andres says he has not met him yet. Andres suggests a next step, and Rosa agrees to send him something after the convention.
